title: Finding the Number of Visible Mountains
summary: Given a 0-indexed 2D integer array peaks where each element peaks[i] = [xi, yi] represents a mountain with its peak at (xi, yi), a mountain is defined as a right-angled isosceles triangle with its base on the x-axis and a right angle at the peak.
statement: Given a 0-indexed 2D integer array peaks where each element peaks[i] = [xi, yi] represents a mountain with its peak at (xi, yi), a mountain is defined as a right-angled isosceles triangle with its base on the x-axis and a right angle at the peak. A mountain is visible if its peak is not inside another mountain (including the border). Return the count of visible mountains.
constraints: Peak [x,y] defines a mountain spanning interval [x-y,x+y].
A mountain is hidden when its triangular region is contained in another mountain, including boundary containment.
Identical mountains hide each other; return the number of visible mountains.
reference_solution:
def count_visible_mountains(peaks):
    intervals=sorted((x-y,-(x+y)) for x,y in peaks);answer=0;farthest=-10**30;index=0
    while index<len(intervals):
        end=index+1
        while end<len(intervals) and intervals[end]==intervals[index]:end+=1
        left,negative_right=intervals[index];right=-negative_right
        if end-index==1 and right>farthest:answer+=1
        farthest=max(farthest,right);index=end
    return answer

hints: Transform each peak into its left and right ground endpoints.
Sort by left endpoint and scan groups of identical intervals while tracking the farthest right endpoint seen.
A unique interval is visible only when its right endpoint exceeds the prior farthest; duplicate intervals contribute zero.
Earlier sorted intervals are exactly the only possible containers, and farthest right summarizes whether one covers the current interval.
